Three flags, all local-first. Nothing is auto-sent — you review every prefilled message before submitting it. macleanup --contact # the contact card macleanup --feedback # opens your mail client, prefilled macleanup --report-issue # opens a pre-filled GitHub issue macleanup --stats # your run history under ~/.macleanup --report-issue gathers the version, macOS version and chip, RAM, bash and Node versions, and the latest log path — entirely on your machine. --dry-run makes macleanup report what it would remove and delete nothing. Every destructive helper in the script checks the flag and prints a [dry-run] … line instead of executing. It is the single most useful flag in the tool, and it costs nothing but the time of one extra run. npx macleanup --dry-run --all

The first run on a new machine. Directory layouts differ; see yours. The first time you run any section. Especially 12, 21, 23 and 24, which judge by heuristics rather than by a fixed path list. Before wiring a command into a script, cron job or CI step. A typo in a section number is much cheaper to find in a preview. After changing a threshold. Lowering --cache-age-days or --idle-days widens what qualifies, sometimes far more than expected.
documents.s: Use it in these four situations, every time

documents.t: The paths each selected section would touch. An estimate of the space that would be freed. Before 4.6.1 a dry run always reported 0 here; it now measures the size of what it would delete. For interactive sections, the candidate list — orphaned data, idle apps, stale build directories, large dormant files — so you can see the actual names before any of them are at risk. The report files it would write. --dry-run combines with every other flag, and it always wins. There is no flag ordering that turns a dry run into a real one.
documents.s: What a preview actually shows you

documents.t: The most useful previews are narrow. Section numbers come from The 28 sections or npx macleanup --list. # Which stale build directories would go, at a 90-day threshold? npx macleanup --only 23 --stale-build-days 90 --dry-run # Which apps count as idle after 60 days? npx macleanup --only 21 --threshold 60 --dry-run # Which files are both 2 GB+ and untouched for 180 days? npx macleanup --only 24 --large-file-size-gb 2 --large-file-days 180 --dry-run # What would a whole profile do? npx macleanup --profile deep --dry-run
documents.s: Preview one section at a time

documents.t: The six deep sections — 6, 10, 11, 14, 21 and 24 — are refused in unattended batch mode unless both --yes and --i-understand-deep are present. A --dry-run preview is always allowed and does not delete files; it still writes its normal log: npx macleanup --only 21 --yes --dry-run # previews; deletes nothing npx macleanup --only 21 --yes # refused in batch mode without --i-understand-deep Since 4.6.0 a dry run also never attempts privilege elevation, so previewing a sudo section does not prompt for your password.

Terminal scrollback is a poor review surface for a few hundred paths. Two better options: # Save it to a file and read it in an editor npx macleanup --only 23 --dry-run --no-color > ~/Desktop/macleanup-preview.txt # Or get a machine-readable summary npx macleanup --only 3,5 --dry-run --json --no-color strips the ANSI escapes so the file stays readable. --json emits a single-line object on stdout — everything else goes to stderr — with freed_kb, sections_done and the report paths. See --json for the full shape. Several sections also write a dated .txt report to ~/.macleanup/reports/ during a dry run, which is often the easiest list to work from. See Reports and logs.
documents.s: Capture the preview so you can read it properly

documents.t: --dry-run is a strong guarantee about macleanup's own behaviour. It is not a promise about your filesystem: It is a snapshot. A preview reflects the state at that moment. If you open a file after previewing, its access time changes and it may no longer qualify on the real run — or the reverse. A real run can find more. Between the two runs, files age past a threshold. Re-preview if a while has passed. Interactive sections still ask. A preview shows the candidate list; on the real run you choose from it. What you select is what goes. It does not validate your judgement. macleanup can tell you a directory has not been touched in 200 days. It cannot tell you whether you need it. It is not a backup. Keep a separate current backup before a large run. If Time Machine is configured, you can also request a local snapshot: tmutil snapshot

macleanup is safe by default and it is still a tool that runs rm -rf and sudo on your machine. Both halves of that sentence are true and neither cancels the other. This page states exactly what the design guarantees, and where the guarantee ends and your judgement begins.
Every destructive section prompts [y/N] before it acts. --yes auto-confirms those prompts; the typed-yes gate on section 14 is independent and is not affected by --yes.
Every destructive call routes through a helper that no-ops in dry mode. See Preview with --dry-run.

Sections 12 and 21 use Finder to move orphaned data and applications to the Trash, so they stay recoverable until it is emptied. Section 24 does the same for large stale files. If Finder fails, the affected item stays in place.
documents.s: 3. App data and apps are moved to the Trash

documents.t: Sections needing root ask for sudo. If sudo is unavailable — or you passed --no-sudo — the section is skipped and reported, never half-run. Sudo-requiring sections: 6, 7 (system logs), 9 (system updates), 11, 13, 14, 20, 25 (system LaunchAgents), and 27 (only the optional system font-cache clear).
documents.s: 4. Sudo sections are skipped, never silently bypassed

documents.t: Six sections are gated: 6 (system caches as root), 10 (Empty Trash), 11 (Time Machine snapshots), 14 (/private/var/folders wipe), 21 (app uninstall) and 24 (large stale files → Trash). They are never part of --all — not even --all --yes. To run one unattended via --only or --profile, you need --i-understand-deep in addition to --yes. --yes alone is refused, with a warning, and the section is skipped. --dry-run previews are always permitted: they delete nothing, although normal logs and reports may be written to disk. Section 14 additionally requires a typed yes. The gate exists so that a one-character typo in a section number cannot trigger an irreversible operation.
documents.s: 5. The deepest sections never run unattended by accident

documents.t: A dated log lands in ~/.macleanup/logs/, and the sections that produce lists write dated .txt reports to ~/.macleanup/reports/. Both live in your home directory, outside any npx cache, and survive every invocation. See Reports and logs.

Introduced in 4.3.3, this governs candidate selection in four sections that can remove non-cache data: 12 (orphaned app data), 21 (idle apps), 23 (stale build artefacts) and 24 (large unused files). An item qualifies only when both hold: It is not in use by any installed software or tool. The per-section detection decides this — no matching installed app for orphan data, no last-used signal and not currently running for an idle app. It meets that section's age threshold — --idle-days for 12 and 23, --threshold for 21, or --large-file-days for 24. All default to 100 days. Sections 12, 23 and 24 check atime and mtime; section 21 uses available app last-use signals and skips apps without a usable signal. Condition 2 is what makes the rule work in practice. A node_modules your editor reads for autocomplete keeps a recent access time and survives. A Gradle distribution you invoke monthly survives. Lowering an age threshold widens the candidate list; review it before confirming a deletion. Sections 16 and 17 are different For iOS backups (16) and Xcode archives (17), --idle-days only highlights idle items with an [idle ≥Nd] marker. There is no automatic delete gate — both are interactive-only and will delete any item you confirm, recent or not.

Section 21 decides an app is idle using five signals in priority order: Spotlight kMDItemLastUsedDate, Saved Application State mtime, Container mtime, Preferences plist mtime, and Spotlight kMDItemUseCount. An app with no usable signal is skipped. The tool deliberately under-flags: missing a stale app is cheap, uninstalling a needed one is not.
documents.s: Idle-app detection, and why it under-flags

documents.t: CRITICAL_HOME_DIRS is a hard refusal list. Section 23 will not enter toolchain-manager directories such as ~/.bun, ~/.pnpm-store, ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm-packages and ~/.volta, regardless of how old their contents look. Section 23 also refuses to scan without roots. If none of the standard dev folders exist (~/Projects, ~/Code, ~/Developer, ~/dev, ~/repos, ~/work, ~/Documents, ~/Desktop, ~/Downloads) and you passed no --scan-roots, it errors out and asks for one rather than falling back to scanning your entire home directory. Both rails exist because v4.3.0 lacked them and broke people's global tooling. That incident, and how to recover from it, is documented in full in Recovery. It is the strongest argument on this site for running --dry-run first. Add your own protected trees with the repeatable --exclude-path: npx macleanup --only 23 \ --exclude-path "$HOME/Code/active-project" \ --exclude-path "$HOME/Code/client-work" --dry-run

documents.t: The script makes no network calls by default. The Node launcher only spawns bash — no analytics, no crash reporting, no phone-home. Logs and reports never leave ~/.macleanup/. The one exception is opt-in: --check-update makes a single unauthenticated GET to https://registry.npmjs.org/macleanup/latest to compare versions. It sends no cleanup paths or reports. npm still receives normal request metadata, such as your IP address. The check times out in seconds and never blocks the run. --feedback and --report-issue open your mail client or a pre-filled GitHub issue for you to review and submit — nothing is sent automatically.

The rules above bound what macleanup does. They do not bound the consequences of a cleanup you asked for: There is no undo. No restore point, no transaction log, no macleanup --undo. The Trash is the only built-in second chance, and only for sections 12, 21 and 24. Deleting the right file at the wrong time still hurts. A stale node_modules is only reinstallable while the lockfile resolves and the registry still has those versions. Heuristics are heuristics. "Orphaned", "idle" and "stale" are informed guesses about your intent. Review the interactive lists. --yes transfers the judgement to you. It is the correct flag for a cron job you have already validated with --dry-run, and the wrong flag for a command you are trying for the first time. Third-party apps can hide data anywhere. An uninstall removes the known locations, not every location. Back up before any cleanup tool runs. A pinned Time Machine snapshot or a tmutil snapshot is the last line of defence that actually works.
What gets deleted — the full inventory, by tier. The 28 sections — per-section confirmations and sudo needs. Recovery — restoring tooling after the v4.3.0 section 23 bug.

macleanup removes files in different ways, and the recovery path depends on the section. Some caches can regenerate. Logs, temp files and app state may contain unique data. Items moved to the Trash can be restored until it is emptied. Direct deletion needs a backup for recovery. This page is the full inventory. Read the three tiers below, then look up the individual sections you plan to run in The 28 sections. Nothing on this page runs by itself macleanup only touches a section you selected — from the interactive menu, or by number with --only, or through --all / --profile. Sections you never choose are never executed.

Tier What happens Recovery 1 — Routine direct removal Caches, logs, temp files and some app state are deleted Some caches rebuild; unique logs, temp data and app state need a backup 2 — Moved to Trash Orphaned app data (section 12), apps (section 21) and large stale files (section 24) go to the Trash Put it back, until you empty the Trash 3 — Permanently deleted Unlinked directly. Snapshots, archives, backups, build directories, Trash contents Your backup only. There is no undo

These entries include caches, logs, saved state or temporary files. They do not all regenerate. Section 4 also offers a separate, irreversible Docker volume prune in interactive mode; see Tier 3. Section 5 can clear saved window state. Section What it removes Notable protection 1 Xcode DerivedData, iOS/tvOS/watchOS DeviceSupport, Xcode Logs, DocumentationCache, com.apple.dt.Xcode cache; unavailable simulators Age-aware — recently built projects survive. Wiping CoreSimulator entirely is a separate opt-in confirm 2 Gradle build caches, Android SDK build caches Age-aware 3 Package-manager caches: npm, yarn, pnpm, Homebrew, pip, CocoaPods, cargo, go, Ruby, Flutter Age-aware. brew autoremove is off by default — see the 4.3.0 note 4 Unused Docker containers, images, networks and build cache Requires the Docker daemon; named volumes are preserved by default 5 ~/Library/Caches entries, ~/Library/Saved Application State, ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports Apple (com.apple.*), every supported browser, password managers (1Password, Bitwarden, KeePassXC) and Caches/node are always preserved 6 Non-Apple entries in /Library/Caches (sudo) Apple caches preserved. Skipped entirely without sudo 7 Old user and system log files (sudo for system logs) Age-thresholded per location — recent logs are kept 8 Old, top-level regular files in $TMPDIR and /private/tmp User-owned files at least two days old only; leaves nested entries and ~/tmp alone 9 Downloaded update caches (sudo) — 19 HTTP and code caches for Chrome, Chrome Canary, Brave, Edge, Vivaldi, Chromium, Opera, Opera GX, DuckDuckGo, Arc, and the Firefox family (Firefox, Dev Edition, Nightly, LibreWolf, Floorp, Zen), across every profile Only cache subdirectories (Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache, service-worker caches). Profile data, history, logins, bookmarks and extensions are left intact. Safari is advisory only — macleanup tells you to clear it yourself 27 QuickLook thumbnail cache and font caches (sudo only for the optional system-wide font clear) Menu / --only only — never in --all Honest note on section 5. Clearing Saved Application State means apps stop reopening the windows you left open. That is a real behaviour change, not a bug, and it is a separate optional confirmation. Honest note on section 19. Clearing browser caches can sign you out of some sites and makes the next page load slower until things re-cache. It does not delete your passwords, bookmarks or history.

Recoverable — but only until the Trash is emptied, including by section 10 in the same session. Section What moves to the Trash 12 Orphaned application-support and container data with no installed parent app 21 Applications idle for at least --threshold days, plus their known companion data — application support, caches, preferences, containers and Group Containers 24 Files at least --large-file-size-gb GB in size and untouched for at least --large-file-days days Section 21 removes companion data too An uninstall is not just the .app. Section 21 also removes the app's known support and container directories. That is what makes it a real uninstall — and it also means the app's local data goes with it. If an app holds documents you care about inside its container, export them first. If Finder cannot move an item to the Trash, macleanup leaves it in place and reports the failure. It does not delete that item directly. macleanup removes the locations it knows about. An application that stored data somewhere unconventional may leave files behind — no uninstaller can promise otherwise.

Nothing here goes to the Trash. When a section in this tier runs, the data is unlinked, and only a backup gets it back. Section What is permanently deleted Why it is here 4 (optional) Unused Docker volumes, only after a separate typed yes in interactive mode A named volume may hold the only copy of a database; batch mode skips volume pruning 10 Everything in ~/.Trash, and the per-user trash on each mounted external volume Emptying the Trash is final — including anything sections 12, 21 and 24 put there earlier in the same session 11 APFS local Time Machine snapshots These are your local rollback points. Deleting them removes the ability to restore recent local changes 14 The /private/var/folders deep cache (sudo) Requires a reboot afterwards. Needs a typed yes, not just y 16 iOS / iPadOS device backups you select A device backup can be the only copy of a phone's data. Interactive review, per device 17 Xcode archives you select Archives contain the dSYMs needed to symbolicate crash reports from already-shipped builds 23 Stale build directories inside your scan roots — node_modules, vendor, dist, .next, target, Pods and similar Reinstallable in principle, but only if the lockfile and network cooperate. A private or yanked dependency may not come back 25 (optional) Selected stale LaunchAgent or LaunchDaemon .plist files They are unloaded and permanently removed. In batch mode, both --yes and --i-understand-deep are required; that combination selects every candidate 13 Runs sudo periodic — macOS's own log rotation and maintenance Not a macleanup deletion as such; macOS decides what it rotates 20 Flushes DNS/mDNS caches and renews DHCP on en0 (sudo) No user data involved; listed for completeness 22 Triggers macOS to reclaim purgeable space macOS decides what to purge Section 14 needs a reboot The /private/var/folders wipe removes per-user temporary state that running processes hold open. macOS behaves oddly until you restart. This section asks for a typed yes, it is never part of --all, and it needs --i-understand-deep to run unattended.

These only read and write a report to ~/.macleanup/reports/. They are safe to run at any time, and --profile audit bundles them. Section Produces 0 System health and running-process overview 15 Installer leftovers report — advisory only 18 Large files report — everything ≥ 500 MB under $HOME 26 Disk-usage report for $HOME and ~/Library

Documents, photos, music and code outside selected cleanup paths. Section 23 can remove files inside a matched build directory; section 24 can select a large stale personal file; section 21 can move app container data to the Trash; section 10 empties whatever is already in the Trash. Review those separately. Browser bookmarks, history, saved logins, cookies-as-profile-data and extensions — section 19 clears cache subdirectories only. Password-manager data — 1Password, Bitwarden and KeePassXC caches are on the section 5 preserve list. Apple system caches in sections 5 and 6. Toolchain manager directories — ~/.bun, ~/.pnpm-store, ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm-packages, ~/.volta and their peers are on a hard allowlist that section 23 refuses to enter. See Recovery for the incident that created it. Anything on a read-only mount, or the boot volume's trash under /Volumes.

documents.t: Two numbers govern whether something old enough to delete actually gets deleted. Both default to 100 days and both look at atime and mtime. Threshold Applies to Flag Cache age Sections 1, 2, 3 --cache-age-days N Idle age Sections 12 and 23 (delete gate); 16 and 17 (highlight only) --idle-days N Because atime counts, a file you merely opened recently survives. A Gradle distribution invoked once a month keeps a recent access time and is kept, even though it was downloaded a year ago. Passing 0 disables the filter and turns the section into a full wipe.
documents.s: The two thresholds that decide most deletions

documents.t: --all is not "everything". It runs the safe batch only — sections 0, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, 18, 22, 26. It does not select any of the six deep sections (6, 10, 11, 14, 21, 24). --profile minimal --yes keeps your Trash. The minimal profile is 5, 7, 8, 9. To empty Trash unattended with section 10, explicitly select it and pass both --yes and --i-understand-deep. Preview any profile with --dry-run before adding --yes.
Preview with --dry-run — see the exact paths before anything is removed. Safety model — the guarantees, and their limits. The 28 sections — per-section detail, sudo needs and flags.

Highlights of each release, newest first. The authoritative, complete changelog lives with the source: CHANGELOG.md. Versions follow semantic versioning. This documentation describes 5.1.0. Verify the published version with macleanup --check-update before installing or updating. macleanup --version # what you have macleanup --check-update # what is published Entries before 5.0.0 use the names that were current at the time.

Released 2026-10-30. Section 26 (disk usage report) no longer measures ~/Music, ~/Movies or ~/Pictures, so the desktop app no longer asks for Apple Music, media or Photos access on a first preview. The report says they were not measured. In the desktop app: an assistant that explains a preview, typed or spoken; receipt backups on Pro and Team; and required updates. Automatic updates now relaunch at a quiet moment, never during a run.
documents.s: 5.3.0 — an assistant, receipt backups and required updates

documents.t: Released 2026-10-30. --exclude-path now keeps a path in every bulk wipe and age-based prune, not only in the per-item deletes; a folder that holds a kept path is left whole. Section 18 skips photo libraries, iCloud folders, Movies, Music, virtual machines and the Trash instead of walking them, so the scan takes seconds. The script is split into an entry file and short modules in lib/; what it does is unchanged. Output names the macleanup team instead of a person. In the desktop app, scheduled runs now report back with a receipt.
documents.s: 5.2.2 — keep means keep, a faster large-file scan

documents.t: Released 2026-10-30. README and package metadata only: the npm page shows the current version and size and links the website as the homepage. The script is unchanged.

Released 2026-10-30. The macleanup desktop app for macOS ships with this release: one disk image for Apple silicon and Intel Macs, running this same script with a disk gauge, a dry-run ledger and a receipt for every run. Section 0 (system health, read-only) lists installed developer toolchains — Node versions under nvm, pyenv Pythons, rbenv Rubies, rustup toolchains, Java VMs, Xcode, the Android SDK and Studio, Docker Desktop, Flutter and Homebrew — with the space each takes. It changes nothing. In the JSON event stream, each item carries age_days, toolchain items carry tool and version, and section 5 names each cache folder it would clear. The schema stays at version 1.
documents.s: 5.2.0 — the desktop app and a toolchain inventory

documents.t: Released 2026-10-30. --json-events prints a newline-delimited JSON event stream on stdout while the run happens: plan, disk, section_start, item, progress, section_result, error and summary. Schema version 1 is on the JSON event stream page. The macleanup desktop app reads this stream. --archive-path PATH (repeatable) writes PATH to a gzip archive in ~/.macleanup/archives/ before it is deleted or moved to the Trash. The folder is mode 700 and each archive mode 600. If the archive cannot be written, PATH is left in place. --exclude-path now protects a path in every section's delete and Trash move, not only in sections 23 and 24. --all runs its safe-batch sections through the same dispatcher as --only, so every run uses one accounting path. The session summary counts attempted, skipped and failed sections beside the completed ones. It also shows the local-snapshot count, with a note that deleted files may not free space until macOS releases those snapshots. Section 12 lists the orphan-shaped entries it skipped because they were touched recently, in its report, for review. A skipped entry is not proof that nothing is left behind. Section 25 lists loaded Homebrew and third-party services in both launchd domains, your user's and the system's. brew services list in one domain can say none while a root service is running. The launcher is verified on Node 14.21.3, so the declared engines.node floor of >=14 holds. The macleanup desktop app is being released alongside 5.1.0. It runs this same script.
documents.s: 5.1.0 — event stream, archives and run accounting

documents.t: Released 2026-10-29. The command, script, data folder, config file and environment variables all use one name: macleanup, macleanup.sh, ~/.macleanup/, ~/.macleanuprc and MACLEANUP_*. Run it as macleanup or npx macleanup. The second command name that earlier versions installed is gone. Scripts and shell aliases that called it need to call macleanup instead. The first 5.x run copies an existing 4.x data folder into ~/.macleanup/ and leaves the original in place. The 4.x config file and environment variable names are still read for 5.x, with a note asking you to rename them. The package no longer declares a main entry, so importing macleanup from Node fails instead of starting the cleanup tool. See Upgrading to 5.0 for the full table.

Released 2026-10-26. Section 25 preserves spaces in structured LaunchAgent program paths. It no longer reports an existing target such as one under Application Support as missing. Ambiguous raw plist strings are skipped; genuinely missing targets still appear in the audit. Section 25 is report-only in batch mode unless both --yes and --i-understand-deep are supplied. The interactive menu always asks which candidates to remove. Previously, --yes alone selected and removed every reported stale launch item.

Released 2026-10-23. The minimal profile no longer selects Empty Trash. Section 10 now needs both --yes and --i-understand-deep when run unattended. A refused deep section no longer appears as completed in the run summary. Section 8 leaves ~/tmp and nested temp entries alone. It removes only old, top-level regular files from the system temp locations. Sections 12 and 21 leave affected data in place when Finder cannot move it to the Trash. They no longer fall back to permanent deletion.
Released 2026-07-25. Corrected the README version row to match the published package version.
Released 2026-07-25. Changed the package license to MIT. Reworked the README to make destructive behavior, recovery limits, and the package's public interface clearer.

Released 2026-06-08. A dry run now estimates the space it would free. Previously --dry-run reported freed_kb: 0: it printed per-folder "would clear …" notes but never tallied a total, so previews showed 0 B. The cleanup helpers and section 5 now measure what they would delete and report the estimate. --json lists only this run's report files. It previously included every file in the reports directory, leftovers from earlier runs the same day included; it now filters to files written during the current run.

Released 2026-06-08. One admin prompt per run for the desktop GUI. When launched by the companion macOS app, the CLI routes sudo through a graphical askpass, so privileged sections (6, 7, 9, 11, 13, 14, 20) actually run from the GUI and ask for the password once. They previously skipped silently, having no terminal to prompt on. Terminal users are unaffected. --dry-run no longer attempts privilege elevation — a preview never prompts for a password; only a real run does.

Released 2026-06-08. --flag=value is accepted, alongside --flag value. A token like --cache-age-days=30 was previously rejected with exit code 2. Clearer unknown-option errors — the offending option plus a one-line hint, instead of dumping the whole help text.

Released 2026-06-08. A broad audit-driven release, with two behaviour changes that matter to unattended users. Ctrl-C now actually aborts. The combined exit/interrupt trap returned without exiting, so on SIGINT/SIGTERM bash ran cleanup and then resumed the interrupted operation — including a destructive one. --i-understand-deep introduced. The deep sections (6, 11, 14, 21, 24) now need this flag in addition to --yes to run unattended. --yes alone no longer enables them, and --all never does. Section 13 removed from the --all safe batch. Running sudo periodic unattended is privileged system maintenance, not cache cleanup. Section 27 added — QuickLook and font caches. Menu / --only only. --json one-line run summary for scripting and CI. --exclude-path PATH — repeatable, protects a tree from sections 23 and 24. --prune-history [N] and --uninstall-data for housekeeping. Config file ~/.mac-cleanuprc — defaults in key = value form, overridden by any explicit CLI flag.

Released 2026-05-13. Defensive hardening of the CRITICAL_HOME_DIRS allowlist, making the pnpm and corepack protections explicit so a future change cannot silently regress them. No behaviour change for anyone whose section 23 had been working correctly.
Released 2026-05-10. A complete end-user documentation set under docs/ in the source repository. No script behaviour changed.

Released 2026-05-10. Feedback channels became first-class, with the no-telemetry promise unchanged — nothing is ever auto-sent. --contact — the author contact card. --feedback — opens your mail client with a prefilled message. --report-issue (alias --report-bug) — collects environment info entirely locally, opens a pre-filled GitHub issue, and copies the last 50 log lines to the clipboard. Nothing is transmitted until you click Submit. --stats — a read-only summary of ~/.mac-cleanup/.

Released 2026-05-10. Anything that is not pure cache must now satisfy both conditions before it is deleted automatically: not in use by any installed software, and untouched (atime and mtime) for at least --idle-days days, default 100. This closed the failure mode where the first condition held but the second was never checked — a container directory whose owning app could not be matched by bundle id, but which something was still touching. Applies to sections 12, 21, 23 and 24.

Released 2026-05-10. Sections 1, 2 and 3 stopped wiping entire caches. They previously deleted every file regardless of recent use, which is what produced reports like "my Gradle distribution disappeared". They now keep anything whose atime or mtime is inside --cache-age-days.

Released 2026-05-10. Anyone still on 4.3.0 should upgrade. Section 23 no longer enters toolchain or config directories. 4.3.0 could match node_modules-shaped folders nested inside ~/.bun, ~/.pnpm-store, ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm-packages, ~/.volta, ~/.asdf and similar, and selecting "all" then broke globally installed tools. Fixed with a hard CRITICAL_HOME_DIRS allowlist of 35+ entries. No silent $HOME fallback. Section 23 now errors out and asks for --scan-roots when it cannot find a standard dev folder. brew autoremove became opt-in via --brew-autoremove. Recovery instructions for machines affected by the 4.3.0 behaviour: Recovery.
Released 2026-05-10. The release that introduced the section 23 bug fixed in 4.3.1. Added profiles and several flags. Do not run this version.

Released 2026-05-09. Published to npm as macleanup, so npx macleanup works with no install. A dependency-free bin/mac-cleanup.js launcher validates Darwin and spawns bash. Both macleanup and mac-cleanup are registered as bin names. Persistent logs and reports moved to ~/.mac-cleanup/{logs,reports}/, out of the repo directory that npm's cache reclaims after an npx run. A branded credits header was embedded in every log and report. New --logs-dir, --reports-dir, --no-reports, --cleanup-logs-on-finish.

Released 2026-05-09. Section 23 — stale build artefacts (node_modules, vendor, dist, build, .next, .nuxt, .turbo, .vite, .parcel-cache, .svelte-kit, .astro, .cache, target, Pods, coverage, .nyc_output), sorted by size with multi-select bulk delete. Section 24 — large stale files, moved to the Trash for safety. Section 25 — LaunchAgents / LaunchDaemons audit. Section 26 — disk-usage report. New --scan-roots, --list, --version, --no-color; multi-select in section 21; hardened path quoting and a bash-version and macOS preflight.

Released 2026-04-17. A complete rewrite into one self-contained mac-cleanup.sh, replacing the previous modular split and four standalone legacy scripts. Identical feature set, with one state, logging and prompt model — and one safe_rm_rf, one clean_dir_contents and one confirm helper shared by every section. --all stopped auto-running destructive sections, limiting itself to the read-only and cache-only sweeps. --threshold N was added, along with per-day rolling logs.

The assistant explains a preview in plain words: what is safe to remove, why a section is large, what a recovery tier means. It sees section numbers, sizes and counts, never a file path or file name.

Open Assistant under Review after a preview. Type a question, or pick a suggested one, such as What is safe to remove? Answers link to the pages of this documentation they rely on. For each section in the preview the app sends only: Sent Never sent Section number, planned size, recovery tier, item count, status File paths, file names, item names, your home folder Answers are guidance and can be wrong. The preview and each section's recovery tier decide what a run changes.

Hold Speak to ask by voice, for up to 30 seconds. The recording is turned into text, which you check and can edit before it is sent. The recording is not stored. macOS asks once for microphone access; typing still works without it.

Plan Level Questions a month Free Spark — fast and efficient 30 Pro Pulse — reasons more carefully 300 Team Surge — thinks deepest 1,000 Questions reset on the first day of each month. When the assistant is resting, it shows when it will be back; previews and runs are never affected. See Plans and allowance.

On Pro (up to 100) and Team (up to 500) you can back up a receipt's summary to your account: Back up this receipt on a receipt, or turn on Back up each receipt after a run in Settings › Backups. On another Mac, sign in and choose Restore to this Mac. A backup holds the receipt's date, macOS and app version, totals and, for each section, its number, status, sizes and item count. It holds no file paths and is not a backup of your files. Deleting a backup, or your account, removes it. See Privacy in the app.

The desktop app is one disk image for Apple silicon and Intel Macs, on macOS 11 or later. It shipped with macleanup 5.2.0 on 30 October 2026. Get it from the download page or the GitHub release. Requires macOS 11 or later Chips Apple silicon and Intel Updates Checked in the app; update packages are signed and verified by the app Command line Not required. npx macleanup keeps working beside the app
Open the disk image. Drag macleanup into Applications. Open macleanup from Applications.

macleanup is not signed with an Apple developer certificate yet, so the first launch may be refused. You allow it once: Open System Settings → Privacy & Security. Scroll to Security. Choose Open Anyway next to macleanup. After that it opens normally.

documents.t: Without Full Disk Access, macOS hides Mail, Messages and some Library folders from the app. Sections still run; they skip what they cannot see and the receipt says so. To grant it: Open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access. Turn on macleanup. Return to the app.

The app checks for updates itself when it starts and every 6 hours. With Install updates automatically on, it downloads the signed update and relaunches at a quiet moment — never during a run. The check contacts GitHub Releases, which receives normal request details such as an IP address. See Privacy in the app.

Sometimes an update must be installed before you continue, for example when it fixes a safety rule. The app checks for a release notice when it starts, every 15 minutes and when you come back to it: Urgent: the app stops and shows the reason with one Update now button. It installs the update and relaunches; your receipts and settings stay. Normal: the app tells you a new version is out and that it is required from the next start. From the next start it asks you to update first. If the notice cannot be read, for example offline, the app keeps working. This website and the documentation use the same notices; there Update now reloads the page.
Plans and allowance — previews are always free. Preview with --dry-run — what a preview does and does not prove.

Every shortcut in the macleanup desktop app can be rebound. These are the defaults. Shortcut Action ⌘ K Open the command palette ⌘ N Start a new preview ⌘ Y Open run history ⌘ , Open settings ⌘ N starts a preview, which changes no files.

One key combination maps to one action. If the combination you choose is already bound, the app names the action that holds it and leaves both unchanged until you pick another. Your bindings are stored on your Mac. Signed in, they also sync with your account and come back when you sign in on another Mac — see Privacy in the app.
Overview

The macleanup desktop app runs the same macleanup script on your Mac, in a window. Every section, profile and safety rule is the one the command line uses. The app makes each step visible: what a run would touch before it starts, and what it did after it ends. Release status The desktop app shipped with macleanup 5.2.0 on 30 October 2026. Get it from the download page. The command line works with or without it.

Screen What it shows Disk gauge Used, purgeable, snapshot-held and free space, so you can see why deleting files does not always free space Dry-run ledger Every path and size before a run. Rows that may be the only copy of some data get a choice: keep, archive or delete Run receipt Attempted, completed, skipped and failed sections, counted separately, with free space before and after Apps and leftovers App bundles, support folders, containers and helpers, with protected items explained Launch items Your account's agents beside the system's daemons and root Homebrew services — both launchd domains The ledger and the receipt come from the JSON event stream the script writes. A row marked as possibly unique is an item event with unique: true. Archives are written to ~/.macleanup/archives/, the same folder --archive-path uses.

Preview first. A preview changes no files. Read the ledger, then decide. The same recovery limits. Trash moves can be undone until you empty the Trash; permanent sections need your own backup. The full inventory is on What gets deleted. The same password handling. Sections that need an administrator password ask for it through MACLEANUP_ASKPASS, the helper the app supplies. One history. The app and npx macleanup share ~/.macleanup/, so logs, reports and receipts from both sit in one place. Prefer the command line? Nothing changes for npx macleanup. It stays MIT licensed and has no run limits.

Install and first launch — Gatekeeper, Full Disk Access, updates. Plans and allowance — what Free, Pro and Team include. Privacy in the app — what stays on your Mac and what syncs. Keyboard shortcuts — the defaults, all rebindable.

File paths never leave your Mac. The app reads folders on your Mac to measure them, shows you the result, and sends that information nowhere. It counts which screens open and which actions run, with Google Analytics; a count never carries a path, a file name or your email. There is no advertising. The command line counts nothing.
Logs, reports, receipts and archives are written to ~/.macleanup/ and stay there, shared with the command line. Settings live in ~/.macleanuprc and in the app's local storage.

An account is optional. Signed in with Google, each run summary syncs only: Synced Never synced Section ids File and folder paths Byte counts File names or contents Statuses — completed, skipped, failed Reports, logs and receipts macOS version Archives The account itself holds your email address and name from Google, your plan, your monthly run count and your saved shortcuts. It is stored with Supabase, the backend provider. Payments go through Polar, which tells the app your plan and payment status; the card number never reaches macleanup. The same rule is a guarantee of the JSON event stream: path appears only in the local stream, log and report.
documents.s: What syncs when you sign in

documents.t: Update check — contacts GitHub Releases. Sign-in and sync — only when you sign in. Checkout — opens in your browser. Release notice — the app reads the newest release notice from the backend provider at start, every 15 minutes and when you return. It sends the product's version and nothing about you. Assistant — only when you ask. It sends your question and per-section numbers, sizes and counts, never paths. Answers come from Anthropic's Claude models through FilesHub; a spoken question is transcribed by Groq and the recording is not stored. See Assistant and backups. Receipt backups — only on Pro or Team, when you back up or restore. The summary is stored privately with FilesHub and holds no paths. Usage counts — a screen or action name and simple numbers, such as how many sections a preview covered, sent to Google Analytics with a random counting ID for the install (and your account's random ID when signed in). Release emails — only when you turn on Account → Emails (app 5.3.2 or later). Your Google address joins the optional release list on FilesHub; the switch or the unsubscribe link in any email takes it off again. Each service receives normal request details such as an IP address.

Account emails (receipts, invites, a scheduled run's result) and rare important product updates, such as a required update or a change to the plans or terms, go to every account. Release news and other optional updates go only to people who ask for them, on the Account screen or the website's download page. The full wording is in the Privacy Policy.

You can download your account data or delete your account from the Account screen. Deleting it removes the account, plan record, synced run numbers and receipt backups from the servers; everything on your Mac stays until you remove it. The full policy is the Privacy Policy.

No cleanup tool can guarantee that. Section 14 (/private/var/folders) particularly warrants care: it requires a reboot afterwards, is behind a typed yes, is never part of --all, and needs --i-understand-deep to run unattended. Have a current backup before running it. Another risk is deleting something you wanted to keep. Read What gets deleted and preview with --dry-run before choosing a section.

No. There is no macleanup --undo, no restore point and no transaction log. Three partial exceptions: sections 12, 21 and 24 move items to the Trash, so they are recoverable until you empty it. Direct deletion needs a backup. A local snapshot may help if Time Machine is configured, but it is not a separate backup: tmutil snapshot

The safe batch excludes the deep sections, but no automated deletion is risk free. Preview the exact command with --dry-run and keep a current backup. --all selects sections 0, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, 18, 22, 26 — and it never runs the deep sections, even with --yes. Be more careful with --profile … --yes. The dev and deep profiles include sections that can delete permanently. minimal leaves Trash alone. See Profiles.

documents.t: Not by intent, and not by any fixed document path list. These sections can reach personal data: Section 24 flags files at or above your size threshold whose atime and mtime are both older than your age threshold. Defaults are 1 GB and 100 days, and matches go to the Trash, not straight to deletion. Section 23 deletes build directories inside your scan roots. If you keep a folder literally named dist or vendor full of documents, protect it with --exclude-path. Section 12 may identify an app's support data as orphaned. Review its list before moving anything to the Trash. Section 21 moves an app and known companion data to the Trash. Export documents kept inside the app's container first. Section 4 can prune Docker volumes containing databases, but only after a separate typed yes in interactive mode. Other sections work from their documented paths and prompts; see the full inventory.

documents.t: No. Section 19 clears cache subdirectories only — Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache and the service-worker caches. Profile data, history, saved logins, bookmarks and extensions are left intact. Password-manager caches (1Password, Bitwarden, KeePassXC) are on section 5's preserve list. Expect slower first page loads and possibly being signed out of some sites, because session data can live in caches.

documents.t: In sections 12, 21, 23 and 24, an item qualifies only when both are true: the section's checks find no current use, and it meets that section's age threshold. Sections 12 and 23 use --idle-days; 21 uses --threshold; 24 uses --large-file-days. All default to 100 days. Sections 12, 23 and 24 check access and modification times; 21 uses app last-use signals. Because access time counts, a node_modules your editor reads for autocomplete survives, and so does a Gradle distribution you invoke monthly. Details: Safety model.
Usually the age filter doing its job — atime counts, so a file you merely opened recently does not qualify. See Troubleshooting for the three common causes and their fixes.

documents.t: Because "all" means "all the safe ones". The batch is caches, logs, temp files and reports. Sections that empty the Trash, delete snapshots, uninstall apps or wipe /private/var/folders are deliberately excluded so that a habitual --all --yes can never become an incident.

It can uninstall formulae that were installed as dependencies and are now considered unused — in practice node, python or openssl — silently breaking every global tool built on them. It has been opt-in via --brew-autoremove since 4.3.1. See Recovery.

documents.t: No, and there are no plans for a port. The script reads macOS-specific paths and calls tmutil, xcrun, dscacheutil, mDNSResponder, launchctl and osascript. It refuses to start on a non-Darwin platform rather than doing something unpredictable.

documents.t: None. The script makes no network calls by default. The Node launcher only spawns bash — no analytics, no crash reporting, no phone-home. Logs and reports stay on your machine in ~/.macleanup/. The single exception is opt-in: --check-update performs one unauthenticated GET to https://registry.npmjs.org/macleanup/latest to compare version numbers. It sends no cleanup paths or reports; npm still sees normal request metadata, such as your IP address. --feedback and --report-issue open your mail client or a pre-filled GitHub issue for you to review and submit. npm downloads the published package into its cache and runs bin/macleanup.js, a small Node launcher that spawns the bundled macleanup.sh through bash. npm reclaims the cache afterwards. Your logs and reports are written to ~/.macleanup/ and are never inside the cache, so they survive.

This walkthrough deletes nothing until step 5. Review the preview and its limits before choosing the first cleanup.

Use a current backup before the first cleanup, especially before a section that deletes directly. If Time Machine is configured, you can also request a local snapshot: tmutil snapshot A local snapshot is not a substitute for a separate backup and may be unavailable when Time Machine is not configured. macleanup has no built-in undo.

npx macleanup --list This prints all 28 sections and exits. Section numbers are the vocabulary for everything else — --only 23 and --profile dev both mean "these numbers". Full detail: The 28 sections.

npx macleanup --dry-run --all --all runs the safe batch — sections 0, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, 18, 22, 26: package-manager caches, user caches, old logs, temp files, update caches, and several read-only reports. With --dry-run it deletes nothing and reports what it would remove, including an estimate of the space freed. Read the output. If anything listed makes you uneasy, stop and look that section up before continuing. Save it if the scrollback is long: npx macleanup --dry-run --all --no-color > ~/Desktop/macleanup-preview.txt

npx macleanup --profile audit --dry-run The audit profile is sections 0, 12, 18, 21, 25, 26: system health, orphaned app data, large files, idle apps, the LaunchAgents audit and a disk-usage report. --dry-run guarantees this first pass deletes nothing. It can still write dated .txt files to ~/.macleanup/reports/. open ~/.macleanup/reports/ These reports tell you where your disk actually went, which is usually more useful than any single cleanup.
documents.s: Step 3 — Run an audit that deletes nothing

documents.t: Start narrow. Section 3 covers package-manager caches. Removed packages may need downloading again, and a package may no longer be available from its registry. npx macleanup --only 3 --dry-run If you are short on space because of old project builds, preview section 23 instead — but read what section 23 does first, because a deleted node_modules is only reinstallable while the lockfile still resolves: npx macleanup --only 23 --stale-build-days 90 --dry-run
documents.s: Step 4 — Pick one section and preview it

documents.t: Drop --dry-run, keep everything else identical: npx macleanup --only 3 The section asks before it acts. Answer, watch it work, and check the space: df -h /

npx macleanup With no flags you get the menu: choose one section at a time, with a confirmation for every destructive step. This is the best mode while you are still learning what each section does on your machine — and the only way to reach the deep sections without the --i-understand-deep flag. When a section asks "Select items (1..N)": You type It means all or a Every item none or nothing Nothing 1,3,5-7,12 Items 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 12 7-3 A reversed range — auto-corrected to 3..7 Out-of-range or junk tokens are ignored.

Once you know which sections suit your machine, pick a cadence: # Weekly, mostly safe. Preview it once before adding --yes. macleanup --profile minimal --dry-run # Developer caches plus stale build dirs macleanup --profile dev --dry-run # Unattended, after you have validated the exact command macleanup --all --yes --quiet --notify Check a profile before automating it --profile minimal now leaves Trash alone. Other profiles can still remove data you need. Always run a profile with --dry-run before adding --yes. More ready-made commands: Recipes.

~/.macleanup/ ├── logs/ │ └── macleanup-YYYY-MM-DD.log └── reports/ ├── orphans-YYYY-MM-DD.txt ├── unused-apps-YYYY-MM-DD.txt ├── large-files-YYYY-MM-DD.txt └── … Logs are kept indefinitely and are small. Prune them when you like: macleanup --prune-history 30 --dry-run # preview macleanup --prune-history 30 # delete logs+reports older than 30 days

macleanup runs three ways, and all three execute the same script with the same flags. Pick by how often you will use it: npx for an occasional cleanup, a global install for a regular one, a git checkout if you want to read every line first or have no Node at all.

Operating system macOS 11 or later. The tool refuses to start elsewhere — there is no Linux or Windows port Shell bash 3.2+ — the version Apple ships, so nothing to install Node.js Only for methods 1 and 2. The git checkout needs none Architecture Apple silicon (arm64) and Intel (x64) Disk The script is a single file, roughly 150 KB

npx macleanup npm fetches the package into its cache, runs the interactive menu, and reclaims the cache afterwards. Nothing is installed permanently. npx macleanup --dry-run --all # preview the safe batch, delete nothing npx macleanup --list # print every section, then exit npx macleanup --version # print the version To force the newest published version, bypassing a stale npx cache: npx macleanup@latest --version Your logs and reports are never inside the npx cache They are written to ~/.macleanup/{logs,reports}/ in your home directory, so they survive every npx invocation and the cache reclaim that follows it. See Reports and logs.

Best if you run cleanups regularly or from cron, where the per-run npx fetch is wasted work. npm install -g macleanup That puts two identical commands on your PATH: macleanup --version macleanup --version # same binary, same behaviour Throughout this documentation the examples use macleanup. Substitute npx macleanup or ./macleanup.sh freely — the argument parsing is identical. Updating and removing: npm update -g macleanup # update npm uninstall -g macleanup # remove the command Uninstalling the package does not remove ~/.macleanup/. To delete that data directory too, run macleanup --uninstall-data before uninstalling, or remove the folder by hand afterwards.

The option to choose if you want to read the source before running it — which is a reasonable thing to want from a tool that deletes files. git clone https://github.com/aoneahsan/macleanup.git cd macleanup chmod +x macleanup.sh ./macleanup.sh The whole tool is two files: File What it is macleanup.sh The entire tool — plain bash, no dependencies bin/macleanup.js A small Node launcher that only spawns bash on the script above; it exists so npx works Open either in any editor. There is no build step, no minification and no bundled binary.

macleanup 5.0.0 uses one name for everything: the command, the script, the data folder, the config file and the environment variables. Run it as macleanup or npx macleanup. Most upgrades need no manual step, because the first 5.x run copies your earlier logs and reports.

Before 5.0.0 From 5.0.0 What happens to the old name mac-cleanup command macleanup command Removed. Update scripts and shell aliases to call macleanup. mac-cleanup.sh macleanup.sh Renamed in the package and the repository. ~/.mac-cleanup/ ~/.macleanup/ Copied once on the first 5.x run. The original stays in place. ~/.mac-cleanuprc ~/.macleanuprc Still read when the new file is absent, with a note. MAC_CLEANUP_LOGS_DIR, MAC_CLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR, MAC_CLEANUP_RC MACLEANUP_LOGS_DIR, MACLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR, MACLEANUP_RC Still read for 5.x when the new variable is unset, with a note. Daily log mac-cleanup-YYYY-MM-DD.log macleanup-YYYY-MM-DD.log New logs use the new name. Copied logs keep theirs.

When ~/.mac-cleanup/ exists and ~/.macleanup/ does not, macleanup copies the whole folder to ~/.macleanup/ and writes a .migrated-from-4x marker inside it. It never moves or deletes the original. --stats and --prune-history then read the new folder. [NOTE] Copied /Users/you/.mac-cleanup to /Users/you/.macleanup. The old folder was left in place; remove it when you no longer need it. If the copy fails, for example because the disk is full, macleanup says so and your older logs and reports stay where they were.

Update any script, alias or scheduled job that calls the old command: macleanup --version # macleanup 5.0.0 Rename your config file, if you have one: mv ~/.mac-cleanuprc ~/.macleanuprc Rename any MAC_CLEANUP_* variables in your shell profile to MACLEANUP_*. When you no longer need the old logs and reports, remove the old folder yourself. This is a permanent deletion, so check the copy first: ls ~/.macleanup/reports rm -rf ~/.mac-cleanup The [NOTE] lines stop once nothing uses an old name.

macleanup is a command-line macOS cleanup and maintenance tool that deletes files from your machine to reclaim disk space. It ships as one bash script with twenty-eight numbered sections — developer caches, browser caches, system and user logs, temp files, orphaned application data, stale build artefacts, large dormant files, unused apps and several read-only reports. You pick which sections run; each destructive one asks by default before it acts, and --dry-run shows the planned cleanup without deleting files. It still writes its normal run log unless you choose a different log location. It is MIT-licensed, makes no network calls beyond an opt-in version check, and requires nothing but macOS 11+ and bash 3.2+. The macleanup desktop app, released with 5.2.0, runs the same script in a window. The command line works with or without it. This tool deletes files Deletion is the point of the tool, and most of it is not reversible. Many caches can regenerate, but logs may be needed for diagnosis. A deleted node_modules, a purged Xcode archive, or an emptied Trash may require a backup to recover. Before your first real run: read What gets deleted, then preview with --dry-run. Check the listed paths and recovery method before you confirm a destructive section.

# 1. See what a safe-batch cleanup would remove — deletes nothing. npx macleanup --dry-run --all # 2. List every section so you know what the numbers mean. npx macleanup --list # 3. Run interactively and choose sections one at a time. npx macleanup No separate install step is required — npx fetches and runs the package. npm may retain its download cache. Your logs and reports are written to ~/.macleanup/ and survive every invocation.

Job How macleanup handles it Reclaiming developer disk space Sections 1–4 cover Xcode, Gradle/Android, package managers and Docker; section 23 sweeps stale node_modules and friends Emptying caches without losing settings Browser caches are cleared per profile; bookmarks, history and passwords are not touched Uninstalling an app completely Section 21 moves the app to the Trash and removes its known companion data, including Group Containers Auditing before deciding Sections 0, 15, 18 and 26 only produce reports; section 25 reports stale launch items in batch mode unless both removal flags are set Scripted, repeatable cleanups --only, --profile, --yes, --quiet and --json make it cron- and CI-friendly

Honesty matters more here than in most tools, because the failure mode is lost data: It is not a backup tool, and it does not create restore points. Keep a verified external backup before a large run. A local Time Machine snapshot can help with some recovery, but it is not a substitute for a separate backup. It is not undoable. There is no macleanup --undo. Items moved by sections 12, 21 and 24 may be restored from Trash until it is emptied; directly deleted items need your own backup. It is not a Linux tool. It reads macOS-specific paths and calls tmutil, xcrun, dscacheutil, launchctl and osascript. There is no Linux port and it refuses to start on a non-Darwin platform. It does not know your project layout. Section 23 deletes build directories that look stale by timestamp. If a directory matters to you and you have not opened it in months, protect it with --exclude-path. It cannot guarantee an app uninstall is complete. It removes the known companion locations for an app; a developer who scattered files elsewhere is outside its knowledge.

Working commands, grouped by what you are trying to achieve. Every recipe that can delete is shown in its --dry-run form first. Drop --dry-run once the preview looks right — the rest of the command stays identical. Substitute npx macleanup, macleanup or ./macleanup.sh freely; the flags are the same.

# Full read-only audit — writes .txt files you can read at leisure macleanup --profile audit --dry-run open ~/.macleanup/reports/ # Per-directory usage for $HOME and ~/Library macleanup --only 26 # Every file ≥ 500 MB under $HOME, with no age filter macleanup --only 18 # System health and what is currently running macleanup --only 0 Start here. documents.t: # Preview the whole developer bundle macleanup --profile dev --dry-run # Developer caches and Docker prune; Docker volume deletion has a separate prompt macleanup --only "1,2,3,4" --dry-run # Xcode alone: DerivedData, DeviceSupport, simulator leftovers macleanup --only 1 --dry-run # Package-manager caches with a tighter age threshold macleanup --only 3 --cache-age-days 30 --dry-run # Docker: containers, images and build cache; volumes require a separate interactive yes macleanup --only 4 --dry-run

Section 23 deletes permanently. Preview, protect what matters, then run. # Every node_modules-shaped dir untouched for 90+ days macleanup --only 23 --stale-build-days 90 --dry-run # Point it at your real project roots macleanup --only 23 --scan-roots "$HOME/repos:$HOME/code" --dry-run # Protect specific trees — the flag is repeatable macleanup --only 23 \ --exclude-path "$HOME/Code/active-client" \ --exclude-path "$HOME/Code/side-project" \ --stale-build-days 120 --dry-run Reinstallable is not the same as guaranteed A deleted node_modules comes back only while the lockfile resolves and the registry still serves those versions. For a repo you are actively shipping, protect it with --exclude-path.

# 2 GB+, untouched for 180 days macleanup --only 24 --large-file-size-gb 2 --large-file-days 180 --dry-run # 5 GB+, untouched for a year macleanup --only 24 --large-file-size-gb 5 --large-file-days 365 --dry-run Section 24 requires both atime and mtime to be older than the threshold. A file you opened recently is not flagged even if you have not edited it in years. If a file you expected is missing from the list, lower the threshold or use section 18, which has no age filter. Selected files go to the Trash, so they are recoverable until you empty it.

# Which apps have been idle for 60+ days? macleanup --only 21 --threshold 60 --dry-run # A year or more macleanup --only 21 --threshold 365 --dry-run # Review and choose interactively (recommended) macleanup --only 21 --threshold 180 The interactive run supports multi-select — all, 1,3,5-7,12, or none. Apps and their companion data move to the Trash. Unattended uninstall macleanup --only 21 --yes --i-understand-deep moves every idle app to the Trash with no further prompt. Preview first, always.
documents.s: Uninstall apps you no longer use

documents.t: # Every cache layer macleanup --profile cache-only --dry-run # Browser caches only — history, logins and bookmarks are untouched macleanup --only 19 # User caches, skipping everything that needs sudo macleanup --only 5 --no-sudo

macleanup --only "1,17" --dry-run Section 1 clears DerivedData and simulator leftovers; section 17 offers Xcode archives for review. Archives hold your dSYMs Deleting the archive for a build you already shipped means its crash reports can no longer be symbolicated. Keep the archives for live releases.

macleanup --only 25 Finds LaunchAgents and LaunchDaemons whose target no longer exists — a common cause of slow logins and mysterious background processes. Sudo is only needed if you choose to remove something under /Library/. In batch mode, the command above reports candidates without removing them. Removing them unattended requires both --yes and --i-understand-deep and selects every candidate, so preview with --dry-run first.

Validate the exact command with --dry-run before it ever runs unattended. # Step 1 — verify macleanup --all --dry-run # Step 2 — automate the verified command macleanup --all --yes --quiet --notify A launchd weekly job, using the global install: # ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.aoneahsan.macleanup.plist runs this: /usr/local/bin/macleanup --all --yes --quiet --no-reports --all is the safe batch only, and it never includes the deep sections — which is exactly what you want from an unattended job.

# Just the number of KB freed macleanup --all --yes --json | jq .freed_kb # Freed space plus which sections ran macleanup --only 3,5 --yes --json | jq '{freed: .freed_kb, sections: .sections_done}' # Fail a CI step if nothing was reclaimed test "$(macleanup --all --yes --json | jq .freed_kb)" -gt 0 --json implies --quiet and puts everything except the single JSON object on stderr, so stdout stays clean for a pipe.
macleanup --profile deep --dry-run --no-color > ~/Desktop/macleanup-preview.txt --no-color strips ANSI escapes so the file is readable in any editor.

macleanup --stats # what is in ~/.macleanup macleanup --prune-history 30 --dry-run # preview a 30-day prune macleanup --prune-history 30 # prune macleanup --uninstall-data # remove ~/.macleanup entirely macleanup --check-update # is a newer version published?
# 1. Snapshot first tmutil snapshot # 2. Preview macleanup --profile deep --dry-run # 3. Run it, minus the sections you want to keep control of macleanup --profile deep --exclude 17,23 --yes
